bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body: Geopolitical Volatility: Cancellations of international/MICE business (INR 7-8cr impact in Q4, ongoing in Q1); Regulatory: GST 2.0 input credit reversals on sub-INR 7,500 rooms impacting margins until ADR threshold breached; Supply Side: Potential new competition in Gift City (1 player announced); Macro: Gas supply disruptions (mitigated via induction/PNG switch); Base Effects: High comparables from events like Aero Show in prior year.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident and Pragmatic: Emphasized 'disciplined execution' and 'record ADRs'; Acknowledged transient headwinds (war, GST) but highlighted structural strengths (locations, domestic demand); Strategic flexibility shown in willingness to acquire assets despite preference for building; Transparent on margin drivers and mitigation strategies for GST.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: GST Arbitrage: 30% of revenue currently exposed to GST input credit reversal because rates are <INR 7,500; management is actively engineering rate increases via 'inclusions' (breakfast, laundry) rather than pure rate hikes to cross the threshold without losing occupancy; Gas Resilience: Rapid switch to induction cooking and PNG prevented any F&B service disruption despite CNG shortages; FTA Mix Shift: Foreign tourist arrival mix dropped to 27% (from normal 30%) but domestic demand fully absorbed capacity, proving the portfolio's defensive nature against global shocks.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- The company moved to a net cash position in FY26: net debt of Rs 601.5 Crs (FY23), Rs 580.9 Crs (FY24) and Rs 595.0 Crs (FY25) turning to negative Rs 110.3 Crs in FY26, with net debt to equity of 12.6x, 7.4x, 5.8x and -0.1x respectively.
- IPO proceeds of Rs 886 Crs including pre-IPO (fresh issue of Rs 759.6 Crs plus a Rs 126 Crs pre-IPO raise to 360-One Alternates Asset Management), issued at Rs 90 per share on 31st July 2025 with the IPO oversubscribed 3.1x.
- Use of proceeds and deployment as of 31st Jun'26: debt repayment Rs 468.1 Crs (fully deployed), buying of UDS from the promoter Rs 107.5 Crs (fully deployed), an unidentified acquisition of Rs 90.0 Crs earmarked for FY27, and general corporate purposes of Rs 220.0 Crs - against a stated total of Rs 885.6 Crs allocated and Rs 666.3 Crs deployed.
- Funding mix for the expansion: 'approximately 60% of the expansion is to be funded through Debt and balance through Internal Accruals', with the FY27-FY28 tranche funded through IPO proceeds plus internal accruals plus borrowings and the FY29-31 tranche through internal accruals plus borrowings; the deck's two funding-split charts show a ~70/~30 split for FY27-FY28 and a 60/40 split for FY29-31.
- Internal accruals of 'Over Rs 1000 Crs.+' are earmarked to fund capex, with internal accruals explicitly defined as EBITDA less finance cost, tax paid, debt repayment and lease rentals - a deliberately conservative definition.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Second largest owner of chain-affiliated hotels and hotel rooms in South India
- Backed by the 40-year foundation and financial strength of parent Brigade Enterprises Limited
- Hotels affiliated to leading international brands (Sheraton, Grand Mercure, Holiday Inn), supporting distribution reach and service standards
- Assets embedded in larger integrated mixed-use destinations such as the Brigade Gateway campus, pairing hospitality with homes, offices, retail and community infrastructure
- Location-led positioning: branding of each hotel is aligned with the characteristics of its micro-market and target customer
- Pricing power evidenced in FY2025-26 by average room rates up 11% and RevPAR growth of 10%, with portfolio occupancy held at 76.1%
- Broad external recognition in FY2026 across hotel, restaurant, nightlife and general-manager award categories at Sheraton Grand Bangalore, Grand Mercure Bangalore and Holiday Inn Chennai OMR IT Expressway

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Travel demand softness and airfare-driven pressure on occupancy — The Board records that portfolio occupancy 'remains nearly at the previous year level amid softer travel demand and elevated airfares', so growth has had to come from rate rather than volume. Hotel earnings are highly operationally geared to occupancy, and a demand air-pocket would hit an owned, fixed-cost asset base directly.
- Macroeconomic and geopolitical volatility, with uneven international arrivals — The Operational Review describes turbulence in global markets ranging from economic slowdowns and geopolitical challenges to cautious investor sentiment, while international arrivals remained somewhat uneven. The cautionary statement lists general market, macroeconomic, governmental and regulatory trends among the factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations.
- Utility and input supply disruption in food & beverage operations — The Board explicitly flags that 'F&B was impacted by gas supply constraints' during the year - evidence that a material non-room revenue stream is exposed to utility interruption that management cannot fully control.
- Single-business, single-region concentration — The BRSR reports hospitality accounting for 100% of turnover with no other business activity, and the Board confirms there is no change in the nature of the business. There is no diversification buffer against a hospitality-cycle downturn, and the operating base is concentrated in South India.
- Currency, interest-rate and counterparty exposure — The cautionary statement names movements in currency exchange and interest rates, competitive pressures and changes in the financial conditions of third parties dealing with the Company among key factors affecting business and financial performance - material for an asset-heavy hotel owner that depends on international brand operators as counterparties.
- Climate change, energy and emissions — The BRSR double materiality assessment identifies energy and emissions as both a material risk and a strategic opportunity, central to the Group's long-term sustainability vision and Net Zero commitment, requiring alignment with evolving regulations and investor expectations on climate risk.
- Water stewardship and availability — Water is identified in the BRSR as a critical operational resource across the Group's construction, lease rental and facility management activities, carrying both strategic value and risk; mitigation depends on efficiency, rainwater harvesting, water-saving technologies and widespread wastewater recycling.
- Talent attrition in a people-intensive service business — The Company states the hospitality industry is inherently people-centric and that its people are its greatest asset, while the BRSR reports a permanent-employee turnover rate of 45.01% for the current year (first-time reporting, with no comparable baseline). Retention and training are a structural constraint on service standards during a period of portfolio expansion.
- Regulatory and compliance burden of a newly listed entity — The BRSR lists regulatory compliance and public policy as a material issue. The Listing Regulations became applicable to the Company only from July 31, 2025, and the BRSR core has not been subjected to reasonable assurance, so disclosure, assurance and compliance processes are still maturing.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers

business.body:
- Described as the 'Second largest owner of chain-affiliated hotels and hotel rooms in South India' and an 'Owner & Developer of hotels in key cities primarily in South India', backed by the '40-Year Foundation and financial strength of Brigade Enterprise Limited (BEL)'.
- The company owns the real estate and affiliates the assets with Marriott International, Accor and IHG brands rather than operating its own brand; the MD attributes pricing power to 'our superior positioning and low competitive intensity across the portfolio'.
- Parentage is presented as an operating advantage: locating strategic land parcels, corporate clientele tie-ups, shared services (HR, accounting, legal), procurement economies of scale, development opportunities within mixed-use projects, and BEL's ability to build hotels cost-efficiently and on time.
- Industry case rests on a Horwath HTL demand-supply mismatch in BHVL's markets: in FY25 the select markets are shown at a 29.0% share of Indian air traffic against a 23.0% supply share of hotel inventory, with only 12.3% of new hotel inventory supply (Apr-25 to Mar-30) coming to those markets and their overall inventory share declining to 19.2% by Mar-30.
- Structural demand drivers cited: domestic tourism of 236 mn (CY2001), 2,322 mn (CY2019) rising to 5,000 mn (CY2030); foreign tourist arrivals 11 mn (CY2019) to 30 mn (CY2037); and South Indian states contributing 65% of IT and ITeS exports in FY24.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Grow with discipline, expanding into attractive markets and building a diversified portfolio across the business, leisure and luxury segments
- Build the portfolio on the principle that location, brand and experience must come together to create sustainable value
- Partner with leading global hospitality brands, which management credits with strengthening operating discipline, service standards and guest experience
- Fund a disciplined expansion pipeline through a balanced mix of internal accruals and debt, using the IPO-strengthened capital base as the platform for the next stage of expansion
- Near term: strengthen presence with the launch of Courtyard by Marriott Chennai WTC while pursuing value-accretive initiatives such as brand repositioning at select assets
- Medium term: add higher-value and luxury assets to enhance portfolio economics
- Create integrated destinations where hospitality both contributes to and benefits from a wider mixed-use ecosystem of homes, offices, retail and community infrastructure
- Maintain presence in high-demand business and leisure markets to support long-term growth
- Apply disciplined revenue management to drive average room rates and RevPAR across the portfolio
- Embed sustainability as a core operational pillar in how assets are designed and operated, driving efficiency, cost resilience and durable value creation
- Uphold prudent capital allocation, strong governance, operational excellence and stakeholder trust as a newly listed company
- The routed governance sections contain no dividend, payout or reinvestment policy statement. What they do establish is the control framework around capital: all related-party contracts and arrangements during the year were in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis, with no materially significant related-party transactions carrying a potential conflict with the Company's interest, and a Board-approved Policy on Related Party Transactions published on the Company's website. Particulars of loans given, investments made, securities provided and guarantees given under Section 186 are disclosed in the notes to the standalone financial statements rather than in the report. Internal financial controls covering the orderly conduct of business, safeguarding of assets and prevention and detection of frauds and errors were tested during the year with no reportable material weaknesses in design or operation, and the Audit Committee reviews their effectiveness. Governance oversight sits with an eight-member Board that is 50% independent, with six committees including Audit, Nomination and Remuneration, Risk Management and CSR, the first two chaired by Independent Directors.
- Achieve water positivity by 2030
- Increase wastewater recycling by 10% year on year
- Decarbonization roadmap to achieve Net Zero by 2045, with rigorous measurement and management of Scope 1 and 2 emissions and tracking of Scope 3 emissions
- Support 100% renewable-powered operations by 2040 by embracing long-term PPAs and expanding on-site solar, increasing overall renewable energy consumption
- Scale up certified green spaces under LEED, IGBC and other frameworks
- Increase water efficiency and rainwater harvesting, adopt water-saving technologies and curing compounds, and use reclaimed water for flushing, cooling and cleaning operations across projects
- Support cleantech innovation through REAP
- Double materiality assessment conducted at Brigade Group level including BHVL's hospitality operations, with BHVL operating under the Group governance framework and the Group's policies and public commitments
- CSR delivered through the Brigade Centre of Excellence & Skills Foundation for hospitality-sector skill development training, alongside tree planting and community development in and around hospitality projects
- Grievance redressal mechanisms in place for communities, investors, shareholders, employees and workers (OHS-related), customers and value chain partners, with complaints reported as resolved and no community complaints during FY2025-26
- Zero-tolerance POSH policy with constituted Internal Committees and year-round training; no complaints filed under the POSH Act during the year, and compliance with the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 / Code on Social Security, 2020
- Vigil mechanism and Whistle-blower Policy with direct access to the Chairman of the Audit Committee and safeguards against victimisation; no complaints received during FY2025-26
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Brigade Hotel Ventures Limited entered FY2026 with an operating base of 9 hotels held across the Company and its subsidiary, located in Bengaluru, Mysuru, Chennai, Kochi and GIFT City, totalling 1,604 keys operational as on March 31, 2026 (8 hotels in the Company and 1 - the 5-star Holiday Inn Chennai OMR IT Expressway - in material subsidiary SRP Prosperita Hotel Ventures Limited). Against that base the Board states that, looking ahead, the Company plans to expand its footprint through the development of 9 additional hotels comprising approximately 1,700 keys - a pipeline slightly larger than the entire existing operating portfolio, which would more than double keys if delivered in full. Management frames the programme as a strategic expansion intended to strengthen and diversify the portfolio across both corporate and leisure segments, rather than as a single-market or single-format build-out. On execution progress, the only status marker the Board gives for the year is land: 'During the year, the Company has progressed with land arrangements for these upcoming projects.' No individual project is named in this routed extract, no city-level allocation of the approximately 1,700 keys is given, and no commissioning, completion or ramp dates are stated; the Board expressly defers the project-level detail, noting that 'A detailed information of ongoing and upcoming projects as on March 31, 2026 has been given in the Management Discussion and Analysis Report' - a table that does not appear in the sections routed here. On funding, this extract carries no rupee capex figure and no explicit statement that a given source is earmarked for the pipeline. What it does record is that the Company completed its Initial Public Offering during the year - a fresh issue of 8,44,12,565 equity shares aggregating up to Rs 75,960 Lakhs at Rs 90 per share (including a premium of Rs 80), with the issue open from July 24 to July 28, 2025 and the shares listed on NSE and BSE with effect from July 31, 2025 - and that the Company retained resources internally, transferring no amount to General Reserves and recommending no dividend for the year, with the Board describing the reserves decision as being 'to augment resources'. The Board also confirms there are no material changes and commitments affecting the financial position of the Company between the year-end and the date of the report, and no change in the nature of the business, so the expansion is an extension of the existing owned-hotel model - developing and owning assets that are run under leading international hotel brands - supported by the 40-year foundation and financial strength of parent Brigade Enterprises Limited. In short: the routed capex extract establishes a credible and sizeable pipeline (9 hotels, ~1,700 keys, land arrangements underway) and the FY2026 funding events around it, but stops short of project names, capex quantum and commissioning timelines, which the annual report itself points to the MD&A for.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- The outlook for the Indian hospitality sector remains firmly anchored in strong domestic demand, supported by favourable demand-supply dynamics and sustained growth across corporate travel, MICE, weddings and leisure segments
- Structural drivers such as the expansion of infrastructure and the decentralisation of economic activity are expected to shape demand patterns over the medium term
- A gradually weakening rupee may enhance India's competitiveness as an inbound destination while encouraging a greater share of travel demand to remain domestic
- Indian hospitality industry revenues are estimated to grow 9-12% year on year in FY2026 despite the high base of FY2025, on persistent demand-supply imbalances
- ARRs for premium hotels are projected to rise to Rs 8,200-8,500 in FY2026, after Rs 8,000-8,200 in FY2025
- Domestic travel is the strongest demand driver, with over 303 crore domestic tourist visits and domestic tourism accounting for nearly 88% of total tourism spending; Indian tourists account for nearly 84% of overall tourism spending
- Foreign Tourist Arrivals reached approximately 9.02 million between January and December 2025, aided by improved air connectivity and an increasingly diversified tourism portfolio
- Supply-side watch item: branded hotel inventory in India is expected to increase from 204k rooms in FY2025 to 315k in FY2030, supported largely by asset-light growth models
- Global hotel chains are deepening their India focus - Marriott International identified India as a major hotspot in Asia Pacific excluding China, with 99 hotel signings and over 12,000 rooms added in 2025
- MICE is emerging as a strategic growth avenue via the government's 'Meet in India' strategy and digital MICE catalogues covering 60+ cities, with a push to develop at least 10 Indian cities, particularly in South India, into global MICE destinations
- Wellness-led hospitality is gaining momentum, with some properties reporting occupancy gains of up to 36% from wellness-focused packages
- Luxury hotels and destination resorts reported exceptional growth during the 2025 wedding season, aided by the 'Wed in India' push to keep celebrations domestic
- Operating momentum: average room rates rose to Rs 7,453, occupancy remained strong at 76.1% and RevPAR grew 10% year on year to Rs 5,670
- Margin lever: management describes EBITDA margins as robust, reflecting a continued focus on cost efficiency and productivity
- Sustainability as a cost lever: EDGE certification of operating hotels reflects over 20% reduction in energy and water consumption, and renewable energy utilisation rose from 50% in FY2025 to 63% in FY2026, driving efficiency and cost resilience
- Management flags that global uncertainties and geopolitical developments intermittently impacted international travel and may continue to create periodic volatility, with domestic demand remaining the primary anchor of growth
- Management describes a strong development pipeline and a clear growth strategy, with the IPO providing a platform that will support the next stage of expansion
- Disciplined expansion strategy supported by a development pipeline with a planned capex of approximately Rs 3,600 Crore, funded through a balanced mix of internal accruals and debt
- Near-term addition to the operating portfolio: the launch of Courtyard by Marriott Chennai WTC
- Medium-term pipeline skew toward higher value and luxury assets, expected to enhance portfolio economics
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Brigade Hotel Ventures delivered robust Q4FY26 with 13% EBITDA growth and record ARR (INR 8,066), driven by pricing power and cost discipline, though margins faced transient pressure from GST 2.0 input credit reversals and geopolitical cancellations. The strategic pivot toward higher-ADR assets (Courtyard upgrade, Chennai launch) and a net cash balance sheet position the company to mitigate regulatory headwinds and capture long-term value from India's structural travel growth.

risks.note: The Board records that portfolio occupancy 'remains nearly at the previous year level amid softer travel demand and elevated airfares', so growth has had to come from rate rather than volume. Hotel earnings are highly operationally geared to occupancy, and a demand air-pocket would hit an owned, fixed-cost asset base directly.
risks.risk: Travel demand softness and airfare-driven pressure on occupancy

risks.note: The Operational Review describes turbulence in global markets ranging from economic slowdowns and geopolitical challenges to cautious investor sentiment, while international arrivals remained somewhat uneven. The cautionary statement lists general market, macroeconomic, governmental and regulatory trends among the factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations.
risks.risk: Macroeconomic and geopolitical volatility, with uneven international arrivals

risks.note: The Board explicitly flags that 'F&B was impacted by gas supply constraints' during the year - evidence that a material non-room revenue stream is exposed to utility interruption that management cannot fully control.
risks.risk: Utility and input supply disruption in food & beverage operations

risks.note: The BRSR reports hospitality accounting for 100% of turnover with no other business activity, and the Board confirms there is no change in the nature of the business. There is no diversification buffer against a hospitality-cycle downturn, and the operating base is concentrated in South India.

The cautionary statement names movements in currency exchange and interest rates, competitive pressures and changes in the financial conditions of third parties dealing with the Company among key factors affecting business and financial performance - material for an asset-heavy hotel owner that depends on international brand operators as counterparties.

The BRSR double materiality assessment identifies energy and emissions as both a material risk and a strategic opportunity, central to the Group's long-term sustainability vision and Net Zero commitment, requiring alignment with evolving regulations and investor expectations on climate risk.

Water is identified in the BRSR as a critical operational resource across the Group's construction, lease rental and facility management activities, carrying both strategic value and risk; mitigation depends on efficiency, rainwater harvesting, water-saving technologies and widespread wastewater recycling.

The Company states the hospitality industry is inherently people-centric and that its people are its greatest asset, while the BRSR reports a permanent-employee turnover rate of 45.01% for the current year (first-time reporting, with no comparable baseline). Retention and training are a structural constraint on service standards during a period of portfolio expansion.
risks.risk: Talent attrition in a people-intensive service business
